turns.t: Doctor, I'm worried. I've been waking at night in a sweat, shaking, and my meter says my sugar's low. It's happened three times this month.
Thank you for telling me, that's important. What does the meter say, when it happens?
Two point eight, once. Three point one another time. I ate some biscuits and it came up.
Do you lose consciousness, or have a fit, when it happens?
No, no, I don't pass out, and I've never had a fit. I wake up myself.
Let's go through your treatment.
Insulin glargine, 20 units at night. Metformin, 1000 mg twice a day. And gliclazide, 80 mg twice a day.
And do you take the gliclazide even when you haven't eaten?
I try to, but if I skip dinner, I sometimes skip it as well. I'm not always sure what I've done.
Thank you for being honest. I'll note that the gliclazide is meant to be twice a day, but you're not always sure. Any allergies?
No, none.
Medical history?
Type 2 diabetes, fifteen years. And high blood pressure.
Any operations?
Cataracts, both eyes, three years ago.
What time do you have your evening meal, and how much? ~
It varies. Sometimes seven, sometimes nine. Lighter, lately, since I've been trying to lose weight. ~
That's the clue. Gliclazide pushes your body to make insulin whether or not you've eaten, and on top of the long-acting insulin, a lighter dinner can send your sugar too low at night. ~
So it's the tablets? ~
It's the combination. I'd say these night-time lows are most likely due to the gliclazide and insulin together with smaller meals.
Do I stop something? ~
I'd like you to cut the gliclazide to 40 mg twice a day and keep the insulin the same for now. Eat a small snack with carbohydrate at bedtime.
Right. Will it get high? ~
Your sugars may run a little higher, which is safer than lows. I'd like to arrange an HbA1c blood test, to see the longer-term picture.
Fair. What if it happens again? ~
Treat with fast sugar, fifteen to twenty grams, a glass of juice, retest in fifteen minutes, then eat a snack. And ring us with your readings.
I'll write it on the fridge. ~
Please do. If you ever can't wake properly or can't treat it yourself, your family should call 999.
Right. Thank you, doctor. Should I carry something sweet in my pocket? ~
Yes, glucose tablets or jelly babies, always. ~

clinical_actions.description: Reduce gliclazide to 40 mg twice a day and have a carbohydrate snack at bedtime
Treat lows with 15-20 g fast sugar, retest in 15 minutes then eat; ring with readings
Family to call 999 if he cannot wake properly or cannot treat it himself
